title: EA-CORPORA-36 — The Thirty-Sixth Seating: Sappho's Reception and the Future Reader — the Translators, Editors and Critics from Hall's Longinus (1652) to Cox (1925), the Ancient Dossier of Remembrance, the Scholarship Open and Walled, the Future-Reader Strata from Dante to the WIPP Markers, and the Jealousy Reading from Lucretius to Hermann
creator: Cranes, Rebekah
description: The thirty-sixth seating of the originals shelf: Sappho's reception and the future reader, seated for the revision of Closing the Fragment and the Sappho Future Reader framework (#1548). Part A, twenty-three seats: the translators, editors and critics of Sappho from Hall's Longinus (1652) and Boileau through the Spectator, Pope, Fawkes, Welcker, Merivale, Mure, Swinburne, Higginson, Symonds, Vivien, Carman, Wharton, O'Hara, Stacpoole, Wilamowitz and Robinson to Cox (1925); the remembrance fragments in their carriers (Dio, Plutarch, Stobaeus, P.Oxy. XV); the Anthology's epigrams on Sappho; Smyth and Jebb; and the Wikipedia sentence on writing for future readers. Part B, nine seats, the future-reader strata the library lacked, from Ennius in Cicero and Dante to Baratynsky and the Sandia WIPP marker report of 1993. Part C, the strata already seated, by reference; Part D, the open scholarship in copyright (D'Angour, Finglass, Garner, the BMCR reviews) fetched, hashed and held by reference, with pointers to the CHS and Brill open editions; Part E, the works behind pay-, access- and rights-walls, declared. Version 1.1 adds Part F, eight seats for the reception study of the jealousy reading: Hermann 1816, Plutarch's Demetrius and Amatorius, Valerius Maximus and Appian, Gellius, Maximus of Tyre, Racine's Phèdre, Smollett, and Wikipedia's 'Sappho 31', with the ancient and modern witnesses already seated (Lucretius, Theocritus, Apollonius, Welcker, Smyth) entered by reference. Each seat in its original language, hashed, with its loci verified in the text layer.
substrate: Human–machine collaborative. Rebekah Cranes is a heteronym of Lee Sharks, the standing authority on the EA-CORPORA deposits. The sources found, fetched, verified, hashed and indexed, the cross-references verified, the absences declared, and the records drafted, in session by TACHYON (Claude, Anthropic) under MANUS (Lee Sharks) direction. methodology: Each seat fetched in session from the source its record names (the Internet Archive, Project Gutenberg, the Text Creation Partnership, Perseus, Wikisource), kept as served, reduced to a text layer by code and hashed into its MANIFEST.sha256; licences read at the file; loci verified by substring in the text layer, in the source's own readings; public-domain status checked against first publication and the author's death, and stated per jurisdiction where it differs. The strata the library already held were verified in their seats and entered by reference. Works not open were declared with their walls. No text corrected by hand. The builders and this body are under rebuild/corpora/ea-corpora-36/.

wiki_article: EA-CORPORA-36 is the thirty-sixth seating of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive's originals shelf, deposited under Rebekah Cranes, the standing authority on the EA-CORPORA deposits, on 7 November 2026. It seats the reception of Sappho and the history of the future reader as public texts in their original languages, for the revision of Closing the Fragment and the Sappho Future Reader framework, whose groundwork is Research Notes Towards the Future Reader (#1548). Part A holds twenty-three seats: the translators, editors and critics of Sappho from John Hall's English Longinus (1652) and Boileau's Traité du sublime through the Spectator, Pope, Fawkes, Welcker, Merivale, Mure, Swinburne, Higginson, Symonds, Renée Vivien, Bliss Carman, Wharton, O'Hara, Stacpoole, Wilamowitz and David M. Robinson to Edwin Marion Cox (1925); the remembrance fragments in the books that carry them (Dio Chrysostom with fr. 147, Plutarch with fr. 55, Stobaeus, the Oxyrhynchus Papyri XV); the Greek Anthology's epigrams on Sappho; Smyth and Jebb; and the Wikipedia sentence on Sappho writing for future readers, pinned at one revision. Part B holds nine seats of future-reader texts the library lacked, from Ennius in Cicero, Dante, Chaucer, Shakespeare's sonnets and Milton through Wordsworth, Keats, Shelley, Stendhal, Dickinson and Baratynsky to the Sandia report on markers for the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (1993). Part C cross-references thirty-six loci in texts the library already held, Homer, Herodotus, Thucydides, the Phaedrus, Horace, Ovid, the Hebrew Bible, Nietzsche and Whitman among them. Part D holds open scholarship in copyright by reference, each work fetched and hashed with its loci verified: D'Angour, Finglass, Garner and three Bryn Mawr reviews, with pointers to Lardinois 2008 and the Center for Hellenic Studies editions. Part E declares seventy-three works behind rights-, pay- and access-walls. Each seat is hashed into its manifest, and eighty-nine loci are verified in the text layers. Version 1.1 (7 November 2026) adds Part F, eight seats for the reception study of how Sappho became a jealous woman: Gottfried Hermann's Elementa doctrinae metricae (1816), which states the jealousy reading as the sense of the poem's last line, answered the same year by Welcker; Plutarch's Demetrius and Amatorius; the Erasistratus story in Valerius Maximus and Appian; Gellius with Valerius Aedituus; Maximus of Tyre; Racine's Phèdre; Smollett's Roderick Random; and Wikipedia's 'Sappho 31', with Lucretius's division of the poem's symptoms and the other ancient witnesses entered by reference.
